detail:
The National Institute on Deafness and Other Communication Disorders (NIDCD) describes Ménière's disease as a disorder of the inner ear that can cause severe dizziness (vertigo), ringing in the ears (tinnitus), hearing loss, and a feeling of fullness or congestion in the ear. It usually affects only one ear, although in 15 to 25 percent of people with the disorder both ears may be affected, and it is more likely to occur in adults between 40 and 60 years of age.

NIDCD explains that symptoms are caused by a buildup of endolymph, the fluid in the labyrinth of the inner ear, a buildup called endolymphatic hydrops that disrupts the normal balance and hearing signals between the inner ear and the brain. Theories about why the fluid builds up can include constricted blood vessels, viral infections, allergies, and autoimmune reactions, and the exact cause remains unsettled. Diagnosis is most often made by an ear, nose, and throat specialist using the pattern of vertigo episodes and hearing tests, since there is no single test for the condition.

Tabs is not endorsing or verifying this material. Talk to your doctor about Ménière's disease symptoms and diagnosis.

summary: NIDCD explains Ménière's disease as an inner ear disorder in which a buildup of endolymph disrupts hearing and balance signals, causing episodes of vertigo, tinnitus, hearing loss, and ear fullness, usually in one ear.
takeaways: symptoms can include vertigo, tinnitus, hearing loss, and ear fullness
a buildup of inner ear fluid is the mechanism sources describe
the condition usually affects one ear, most often in adults 40 to 60
title: Ménière's Disease: when inner ear fluid disrupts hearing and balance
